title: Lesson 18: The Financial Model: Units, Margins, and Runway
description: How a practice models the units it actually sells and their per-unit contribution, the practice margin left after its fixed base, and the runway that decides whether the compounding choice is affordable.

questions.question: Per the lesson “The Financial Model: Units, Margins, and Runway”, why should a practice model at the unit level instead of in annual revenue and profit?
options: Because yearly totals hide the fixed costs that unit modeling exposes.
Because the unit is where the levers live, a single price, a single delivery cost, a single sales volume, which is what lets the model answer what-if questions.
Because unit economics are required by lenders before a practice can raise cash.
Because annual profit is too volatile to be modeled at all.
questions.explanation: The lesson says you cannot act directly on annual profit, but you can act on one unit's price, cost, or volume, which is what the model is built to test.

questions.question: Per the lesson “The Financial Model: Units, Margins, and Runway”, Delta Forge shows healthy per-unit contribution and a practice margin of about 142,000 a year, but a stress-case runway of only about 4.8 months. What is the founder's correct first job?
options: Build a fourth rung of the ladder, since the healthy margin proves the firm can afford it.
Raise the price of the flagship build so the buffer grows faster.
Cut the fixed base below the six-month line by letting a lead go.
Bank a larger cash buffer and book retained, recurring units that lower net burn, because below the runway floor the compounding choice is not affordable.
questions.explanation: The lesson concludes that margin is the fuel and runway is the tank, so the founder must refill the tank before spending the fuel on a non-delivery bet.

questions.question: Per the lesson “The Financial Model: Units, Margins, and Runway”, what distinction does the lesson draw between modeling and forecasting?
options: Keep the model rigorous, the prices, costs, contributions, fixed base, and runway formula, and keep the forecast humble, since the forecast is always wrong in the details.
Model monthly and forecast annually, because yearly forecasts are more accurate.
Model the units and forecast the runway, because runway cannot be modeled.
Model conservatively and forecast optimistically so the firm is not under-investing.
questions.explanation: The lesson says to spend attention on the structure you control rather than pretending the revenue forecast is precise.
